transcript: Chapter 17 I was born at a place called Lowry Bend, said Rook, which is about 400 miles south and east of here, in country you've never heard of and wouldn't like, and there were 140 of us in it, and my mother did nothing with her hands. I'll explain that. In your part of the world, you've got 11 stones for 400 people, and every one of them's got a history attached, and a person who hasn't got one and can't get one is a person nothing happened to. Where I'm from, there wasn't a stone within 60 miles. Nobody had one. Nobody had ever had one, and if you'd put one on the table at Lowry Bend, the general opinion would have been that it was a clever bit of old-world rubbish and a poor substitute for doing the thing properly. We did it with our hands. That's all it is. You've seen it. The woman in the cut with the wall. That's the same trade. That's my whole village. My mother could put her hands on a rip in a cow and have it hold for a week. My grandmother could do a wall about eight feet across and hold it for four minutes, which in my family made her the greatest woman who ever lived, and I was raised on stories about that wall the way this one. He tipped his head at Torrin without looking at him, was raised on stories about a disc, and I could do nothing at all. He said it without any particular weight. Thirteen. Doors were open. A whole village of people who do it with their hands, and I sat in my mother's kitchen and put my hands out and got nothing for eleven months. Not a wall. Not a mend. A smell of hot metal once that I think I imagined. He turned his head very slightly toward the stone where Dessa was sitting. So you and I have that in common, and I've known it since Hob's Wall, and I've never said a word about it to you, which is one of about nine things I'm going to be answering for tonight. Dessa did not say anything at all. Torrin, sitting four feet from her, heard her breathe out very slowly through her nose. My mother's lungs went in the winter I turned fourteen. It wasn't the radiation. It was ordinary. It was wet and cold and a bad chimney and forty years of it. She could do a mend on a cow, and she couldn't do one on herself. That's not irony. It's just how it works. You can't get the angle. And there was nothing at Lowry Bend, and nothing at the Market Town, and nothing anywhere we could walk to. Then men came through in the spring with a wagon, and a proper doctor sitting on it. They were from a place called Homura. He let the word out into the firelight, and it sat there, and Torrin thought, there it is. That's the first one. That's a name that's never been said in front of us. They had a valley two hundred miles north, up against a fracture. That's a place where the tearing's constant, where you get weather out of it, where the ground hums. Nobody lives at a fracture. They'd built it one on purpose. And what they were doing there was studying what the kindling actually does to a person's head. And they were doing it with instruments. And they had the only working instruments of that kind that I have ever heard of before or since. They wanted subjects. That's the word they used. And they used it to my face on the first day, which I have thought about a great deal since, because they could have said students, and they didn't. They wanted young ones, because it's clearest in the young. They wanted them from everywhere. And that was the thing about Homura. That's the whole of what Homura was. And I want you to hear it properly. They did not care which door you came through. They took stone tradition children off the coast and hand tradition children out of villages like mine. And they took two boys from a monastery in the east who'd never touched either and did the whole thing sitting still in a room. And they put every one of us through the same machines and wrote it all down in the same book. Nobody does that. You've been in exactly one settlement that isn't yours. And you'll be in 40 more before you're grown. And every one of them will have picked one door and decided the other two are a trick, a toy, or a heresy. You see, Hob's Wall weighs you. Lowry Bend would have laughed at that stone in your pocket. It is the oldest and stupidest argument in the world and the whole world is in it. Homura was one valley where it wasn't happening. And they paid? Said Wyke. It was the first thing anybody had said and Rook did not look annoyed about it. They paid, he said. They paid in what a family like mine actually wanted which wasn't coin. A doctor twice a year at Lowry Bend for everybody, as long as I was there. Medicine off the wagon. A name on a list somewhere that meant if the fracture threw something big at us, somebody who owed us would come. I went in the autumn, I turned 14, and my mother stood at the top of the lane and did not cry until I was out of sight. And I know that because my brother told me nine years later, and it is one of about four things I have left of her. Milo made a small sound. So the answer to your question, said Rook, is that I sold myself for five years of medicine for a sick woman who couldn't walk to a wall. And then I walked north with a stranger and I have been on the road with a cart and a sick old woman in it for 27 days. And I would like all five of you to understand that I have known exactly what I was doing every single day of it. Nobody said anything for a while. Senna in the cart had put her mug down. Homura was a valley with wire around it and 11 buildings in it and about 60 people, of whom 40 were us. It was the best place I have ever been in my life. I want that said before the rest because everything else I've got to tell you will make it sound like a hard place. And it wasn't. There was hot water. There was a stove in every room and a cook who thought 40 children was a personal challenge. Nobody hit anybody. They taught us to read properly. All of us, including the ones who came in at 16 and were ashamed about it. And they did it in the evenings and never once made a thing of it. And every day they put us through the machines and asked us to do our tricks and wrote down what happened in our heads while we did them.
